meta.title: Who originally recorded "The Tide Is High"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Blondie. The Paragons recorded it first, in 1967 for Duke Reid's Treasure Isle label, written by their lead singer John Holt.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'The Tide Is High'?
meta.ogDescription: Blondie's 1980 No. 1 is a cover. The Paragons cut it first in 1967 on Treasure Isle, written by John Holt.

answer.label: Not a Blondie original — a 1967 single by The Paragons
answer.originalArtistDates: Jamaican rocksteady vocal group, formed in Kingston in the 1960s
answer.sourceLine: Blondie’s 1980 recording was a US and UK No. 1 and is routinely filed as a Blondie song. It is a cover. “The Tide Is High” was written by John Holt and first recorded by his group The Paragons in 1967, produced by Duke Reid for his Treasure Isle label in Kingston — and issued as the B-side of the single “Only a Smile.” The original was popular in Jamaica and, after U-Roy’s 1971 deejay version, among West Indian and skinhead audiences in Britain, but it went largely unnoticed elsewhere until Blondie picked it up.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Treasure Isle
original.released: Issued in 1967 as a 7-inch single on Duke Reid’s Treasure Isle label (and on Trojan in Britain), as the B-side of “Only a Smile.” It also appears on the group’s Treasure Isle album On the Beach.
original.charted: No international chart placing. It was a hit in Jamaica and circulated among West Indian and skinhead record buyers in Britain — especially after U-Roy’s 1971 deejay version — but it did not chart in the US or UK.
original.cover: Blondie’s version, produced by Mike Chapman for the album Autoamerican, was released as a single on Chrysalis on 31 October 1980. It reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the band’s third US chart-topper — and No. 1 in the UK, Canada and New Zealand.

docMeta.dd: Treasure Isle (Trojan in the UK), produced by Duke Reid

trail: The Paragons cut it in 1967 for Duke Reid at Treasure Isle, backed by Tommy McCook and the Supersonics — per Wikipedia’s entry on the song ↗.
John Holt, who wrote it, sang lead on the Paragons record before going solo around 1970 and becoming a major reggae star in his own right — see his biography ↗.
Cover databases file every later version, Blondie’s included, beneath the Paragons recording — WhoSampled lists them from the 1967 source ↗.

authors.name: The Paragons
authors.heading: The Paragons
authors.bio: The Paragons were a Kingston vocal group who came up through ska and hit their peak in the rocksteady years, recording for Duke Reid at Treasure Isle from the mid-1960s. The line-up that cut “The Tide Is High” paired lead singer John Holt with Garth “Tyrone” Evans and Howard Barrett. Their Treasure Isle catalogue — “Ali Baba,” “Tonight,” “On the Beach” — has been mined by reggae and pop acts ever since. Holt left for a solo career around 1970 and the group carried on in various forms into the 1980s.

authors.name: Blondie
authors.heading: Blondie
authors.metaLine: American new wave band, formed in New York in 1974
authors.bio: Blondie recorded “The Tide Is High” with producer Mike Chapman at United Western Recorders in Hollywood for their fifth album, Autoamerican. Released as a single on Chrysalis on 31 October 1980, it became their third US No. 1 and a UK No. 1 as well, topping charts in Canada and New Zealand too. The arrangement — horns, strings, an unhurried lilt — is a genuinely loving reading of a Jamaican record rather than a flattening of it. The only error in the popular memory is chronological: the band found the song, they did not write or first record it.

authors.name: John Holt
authors.heading: John Holt
authors.bio: John Holt was born in Kingston in 1947 and joined The Paragons in the mid-1960s, singing lead and writing much of their best material, including “The Tide Is High.” He went solo around 1970 and became one of reggae’s biggest voices, working with producer Bunny Lee; 1,000 Volts of Holt gave him a UK Top 10 hit and his smooth, romantic style helped point the way to lovers rock. Jamaica awarded him the Order of Distinction in 2004. He died in London in 2014.

misattribution.heading: Setting the record straight
misattribution.intro: Blondie’s 1980 chart-topper is so dominant that the song is often assumed to start there. It starts in a Kingston studio in 1967.

items.why: Their version, produced by Mike Chapman for Autoamerican and released on Chrysalis on 31 October 1980, went to No. 1 in the US and the UK. It is a cover of a record that already existed.
Recorded for Duke Reid at Treasure Isle in Kingston and issued on a 7-inch as the B-side of “Only a Smile.” Popular in Jamaica, largely unheard elsewhere.
The Paragons’ lead singer wrote it. Publishing registrations, including MusicBrainz, also carry his bandmates Tyrone Evans and Howard Barrett on the composition.

misattribution.truthLine: Right band, wrong century of the song’s life: Blondie made it famous in 1980, but The Paragons made it in 1967.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The Paragons’ record was not a failure — it was a hit in the place it was made. What it never had was distribution. A 7-inch on Duke Reid’s Treasure Isle in 1967, tucked on the flip of “Only a Smile,” travelled as far as Jamaican sound systems and the British record shops that served West Indian buyers, and no further. U-Roy’s 1971 deejay version pushed it further into UK circulation, still inside the same audience.

Blondie were plugged into exactly that circuit through New York’s reggae import shops, and their version arrived attached to a major label, a hit album and international radio. The song did not get better in 1980; it got a passport. The irony is that the 2002 Atomic Kitten UK No. 1 is now widely understood to be “a cover of Blondie” — a cover of a cover, with the actual first recording another step further out of view.
detailsBody: 1967 — The Paragons record “The Tide Is High,” written by John Holt, for Duke Reid at Treasure Isle in Kingston. Tommy McCook and the Supersonics back them; the distinctive violin is played by “White Rum” Raymond.
1967 — It is issued as a 7-inch on Treasure Isle (and Trojan), as the B-side of “Only a Smile.”
1971 — U-Roy cuts a deejay version, which spreads the tune among West Indian and skinhead audiences in Britain.
31 October 1980 — Blondie release their version as a single on Chrysalis, from the album Autoamerican, produced by Mike Chapman. It goes to No. 1 in the US and the UK.
2002 — Atomic Kitten take a rewritten version to UK No. 1; Kardinal Offishall has a minor hit with his own reading in 2008.
context.pull: The song did not get better in 1980. It got a passport.
